releases.headline: A missing object is `objectstore/not-found` on every backend
releases.summary: `b.storage.exists` returns `false` when the backend reports `objectstore/not-found` and propagates anything else, so a transient outage is never read as absence. Only the local and S3 backends produced that code: on Azure Blob and GCS a missing key surfaced as a raw HTTP failure, so `exists` threw where it documents `false`. Every backend now reports a missing key the same way.

items.title: `b.storage.exists` threw on Azure Blob and GCS instead of returning `false`
items.body:
`exists` calls the backend's `head` and returns `false` on `objectstore/not-found`. The local and S3/sigv4 backends mapped a missing key to that code; Azure Blob and GCS re-threw the transport's own error, carrying `statusCode: 404`. An operator gating a downstream write on `exists` got an exception rather than a boolean, on two of the four shipped backends.

A 404 on a `get`, `getResponse` or `head` is now `objectstore/not-found` on every HTTP backend — S3/sigv4, Azure Blob, GCS and http-put — mapped in one place rather than in each of them. The mapped error still carries `statusCode: 404`, so a caller that reads the status instead of the code is unaffected. Nothing else is remapped: any other status propagates exactly as before, which is what keeps a 503 from being read as absence.

On the HTTP backends the code means "the object endpoint answered 404". A provider returns that for a missing container or bucket as well, and a HEAD carries no body while the error carries no response headers, so the two are not distinguishable at this layer. `b.storage.exists` returning `false` therefore means the object is not readable at that path rather than that the store is healthy and the object absent; its documentation now says so. That was already the behaviour on S3/sigv4 before this release, and the other backends now match it.

The same gap was present on the S3/sigv4 `get` path, where only `head` had ever mapped it.

items.title: An ICAP error verdict from `b.mail.scan` now names its error
items.body: `errorCode` and `errorMessage` were added to clamav-instream error verdicts in 0.19.6, and an ICAP error verdict carried neither, so a caller handling `verdict: "error"` had to know which backend answered before it could find out what went wrong. An ICAP response the reader classifies as neither clean nor infected now reports `mail-scan/icap-status` with the status line, and still carries the parsed `icapResponse` alongside it. A clean or infected verdict carries no error fields, as before.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.6.55
items.body: `lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` carries 0.6.55, refreshed through `scripts/vendor-update.sh`, with the `MANIFEST.json` SHA-256 hashes regenerated alongside it. The certificate, PKI and WebAuthn paths that read it are unchanged here.

items.title: Seventeen comments in the shipped source were half-sentences
items.body: The 0.19.0 comment sweep removed lines from multi-line comment blocks and, where it removed only part of one, left the remainder behind. Seventeen blocks in `lib/` ended mid-sentence or opened mid-clause. `lib/` ships in the package, so these were visible to anyone reading the installed source. Each is now a complete statement or is gone.

releases.headline: A scan error says which error it was
releases.summary: `b.mail.scan` on the clamav-instream backend answered every failure with `{ verdict: "error", threats: [] }` and nothing else, so a message too large for the daemon to scan and a daemon that was down arrived identically. A refusal on size will never succeed on retry and a fault clears when the daemon returns, so the two call for different handling. A clamav-instream error verdict now carries `errorCode` and `errorMessage`. An ICAP error verdict is unchanged and still reports its reason through `icapResponse`.

items.title: `errorCode` and `errorMessage` on a clamav-instream error verdict
items.body:
An error verdict from the clamav-instream backend now names which error it was. `mail-scan/clamav-size-limit` is a stream past the daemon's `StreamMaxLength`, which depends on the size of the message and will not succeed on retry. `mail-scan/clamav-error` is a daemon fault, which clears when the daemon returns. `mail-scan/clamav-unparsed-reply` is a reply the framework could not classify as any of clean, infected or error.

`errorMessage` carries the daemon's own words for the failure, truncated to 200 characters because the length of that reply is the daemon's to choose.

The fields are additive and the `verdict` values are unchanged, so a caller that branches on `verdict` alone behaves as before. The ICAP backend already returned the parsed response with its status code, and a scan that threw already set `errorCode`; the clamav-instream resolutions were the only ones answering with nothing.

items.title: A clamd reply that arrives before a reset is kept
items.body:
clamd closes the connection as soon as a stream passes `StreamMaxLength`, while the framework is still writing chunks, so the size-limit reply can be followed by a connection reset with no clean end. The reply was read only on a clean end, so on that path it was discarded and the caller received `mail-scan/transport` for a message the daemon had already answered about, which invites the retry the size-limit code exists to prevent.

A reply that arrived is now used whatever the socket does next, on one condition: clamd terminates a reply with a NUL or a newline, and only a terminated reply is read. Bytes a reset cut in half stay a transport failure, because `stream: OK.` is also the start of an infected reply whose signature name begins `OK.`, and reading it as clean would report a clean scan of a message that was never fully scanned.

The ICAP backend deliberately does not do this. An ICAP response declares an encapsulated body length that the parser does not check against the bytes present, so headers followed by a reset would parse as a complete clean response. A reset ICAP scan stays a transport failure.

releases.headline: An option that governs nothing is refused instead of accepted
releases.summary: `b.guardSql` declared seven options that no code read. Setting `allowMultiStatement: true` read as permission to send a stacked statement and granted none; six more named actions the guard never consulted. Each is now either governed, pinned to the one value it takes, or refused by name. No verdict changes: all 180 across the three profiles and three context modes are identical.

items.title: `b.guardSql` options that governed nothing
items.body:
Every profile declared `rceFile`, `fdw`, `literal`, `privPivot`, `stacked`, `encoding` and `allowMultiStatement`, and no code read any of them. An operator could set one, see no error, and get no change.

Three describe behaviour that is real and fixed. A stacked statement and invalid encoding refuse in every profile, and this guard permits one statement; `stacked`, `encoding` and `allowMultiStatement` are pinned to those values now, so setting another is refused at the door with the option named. `allowMultiStatement: true` is the one that read as permission, and it is refused rather than ignored.

Four named groups of the OS-reach floor detectors that are not separately governed. `floor` is the one control over those 29 detectors and `allowLiterals` governs an embedded literal, so `rceFile`, `fdw`, `literal` and `privPivot` are refused by name, each error naming the option that does govern the behaviour. An unknown option is accepted across the guard family, so an operator carrying one of these forward would otherwise get silence from a guard they had just configured.

Nothing decides differently. The fallback a detector took when its family matched no profile key was `privPivot`, which no detector could reach; it is the floor's action now, which is what every detector already received. Every verdict over a corpus reaching each detector family, in three profiles and three context modes, is unchanged.

`b.guardSql.validate`'s documented options now list every action a profile takes, including the three that are fixed.

items.title: A policy vocabulary can pin a value that is not a string
items.body: `b.gateContract.policyVocabulary` states which values an option accepts, and the check behind it required the value to be a string before consulting the list. An option fixed at a boolean could not be stated, which is why `allowMultiStatement` was left out of the vocabulary and then accepted and ignored. Membership in the list decides it now. A value outside the list is refused as before, whatever its type.

items.title: Vendored public suffix list moves to the 2026-09-07 20:57 snapshot
items.body: `lib/vendor/public-suffix-list.dat` carries the list published as `2026-09-07_20-57-11_UTC`, from commit `9fc6745c5d3f678a59af9c24de72e5eb3c300e2c`. The domain content is identical to the snapshot 0.19.4 shipped; the published stamp is what moved. `b.guardDomain` and the cookie and origin checks that read a registrable domain use it.

items.title: Sixty-one private helpers nothing read
items.body:
Across 49 files, private helpers and bindings that no code reached. Five sat in security guards, where the sharper risk is a defence written and never wired; each was checked and each was superseded rather than missing. `guard-json._stripPollutionTree` duplicated the `strip` pollution policy that `safeJson.parse`'s reviver already applies. `archive-tar._parsePaxRecords` was byte-identical to the one the reader uses. `network-tls._ctLargestPowerOf2LessThan` was the recursive form of a value the iterative consistency-path check does not need. `audit._readAllAuditRowsAsc` was superseded by the live `verify()` queries. `guard-sql._profileActionFor` collapsed to the same value in all three profiles.

One mechanism went whole rather than by instance: a soft-fail helper, its accumulator and the gate that read it, in the Postgres cluster integration test. Nothing called the helper, so the gate could never fire.

The lint rule that reports these was exempting every name beginning with an underscore, which is the convention every private helper in the framework follows, so it exempted all of them. It now exempts only a binding named exactly `_`.

releases.headline: One reader decides which slashes open a pattern, so stripping comments cannot delete a file
releases.summary: Two readers in the test substrate each decided whether a `/` opens a pattern or divides, from their own state, and they had drifted apart. The comment stripper is the one where a wrong answer costs the most: a slash it reads as an opener swallows to the next slash, and where that span holds a `/*` the rest of the file goes with it. Both now read the same table, and the answer is checked by comparing them over the forms the gate's crossings generate rather than over a list of shapes.

items.title: Vendored public suffix list moves to the 2026-09-07 snapshot
items.body: `lib/vendor/public-suffix-list.dat` carries the list published as `2026-09-07_08-55-04_UTC`, from commit `24fdb5107983c3997144ca19e0d7e1e8fc714f03`, up from the `2026-09-05_20-59-48_UTC` snapshot 0.19.3 shipped. The domain content is identical between the two; the published stamp is what moved. `b.guardDomain` and the cookie and origin checks that read a registrable domain use it.

items.title: Vendored PKI bundle moves to 0.6.54
items.body:
`lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` carries `@blamejs/pki` 0.6.54, up from the 0.6.51 that shipped in 0.19.3. This is shipped code: `b.mtlsCa` and `b.auth.passkey` run it.

0.6.52 opens a centrally generated private key delivered in a CMP response, undoing the two CMS layers in order and authorizing the authority before any key material is returned. 0.6.53 derives the public key of a composite ML-KEM private key across all twelve registered families, each checked byte for byte against the test vectors the draft publishes, and that derived key is the recipient the rest of the toolkit accepts. 0.6.54 completes an unsigned enrollment for a composite ML-KEM key: the challenge must still be addressed to the key the request asks for, and where the running engine cannot read that key the canonical composite encoding answers instead of a key object.

There are no API changes and nothing to do on upgrade. The bundle ships with no dependencies and no install hooks, and its recorded SHA-256 is checked against the file on every build.

items.title: The comment stripper and the tokenizer give one answer
items.body:
`_shape-match.js` holds two readers of JavaScript. Both must decide whether a `/` opens a pattern or divides, and each carried state the other lacked: the tokenizer learned to read a function body, an arrow body, a template substitution and a contextual keyword, and the stripper did not. Put to the forms the gate's crossings generate, the two disagreed on 397 of 2,472.

The cost is not symmetric. A slash the stripper reads as an opener swallows every character to the next slash. `var await = 4; await / 2; var re = /[/*]/; var after = 1;` is valid source where `await` is an ordinary name, and stripping it produced `var await = 4; await / 2; var re = /[`: the tail of the file was gone, and what remained did not parse. The same held for a substitution reading `await` as an operator.

Which slashes open a pattern is now answered in one place, for both readers and for the reader that extracts pattern literals. That place walks into a template substitution too, to any depth, since a template is one token and a pattern written inside one reaches no caller reading pattern tokens. Over the 1,392 files in the tree the stripper's output is unchanged and all 9,072 literals are the same ones; the second copy of the substitution walk is gone.

Whether they agree is now a check rather than a claim: the same crossings that drive the other sweeps are put to both readers, and any form where their answers differ is reported.

The patterns are collected while the source is read rather than looked for again afterwards. Finding where a template ends already reads each of its substitutions, so a pattern inside one is recorded there; reading them back walked every nesting level again, and 800 nested substitutions took 99ms against 1.3ms for one pass, 1,600 staying flat. Stripping the 1,378 source files in the tree, 29.8 MiB, takes 1.39s where it took 0.61s.

A region the reader could not read is named rather than left out of the answer. Past the nesting depth its stack carries, a substitution's end is found by counting braces and nothing inside it is read: the patterns found elsewhere in the file are still reported, and that one range is reported as unread. The check that measures patterns for linear time reports such a region rather than reading it as a file holding none, and the comment stripper copies it as it stands rather than answering for it. Guessing there is a guess in both directions, since a division read as a pattern opener swallows to the next slash and a pattern read as division lets a `/*` inside it open a comment, and either can take the rest of the file.

The range runs to the end of the source. Where a substitution ends is then only a brace count, which counts a brace written inside a pattern as structural, so a reader resuming at it resumes in the wrong place: `/\{[/*]/` inside such a substitution moved the resume point and left the block comment after it standing. What this costs is that comments past that point are not stripped, so a check reading the stripped source sees them as code. The framework holds no template nested anywhere near that deep.

items.title: A label is a label whatever word it is spelled like
items.body: `break` and `continue` take a label and nothing else, so a slash after one opens a pattern. The tokenizer asked that only of an identifier, and `async`, `from` and `as` are in its keyword table, so `break async` followed by a line break and a pattern read the slash as division and swallowed from its opening slash. The rule now reads the label whatever word it is spelled like, which is how the same file already reads a class or function name.

items.title: A bare arrow's body ends a statement
items.body: `var q = () => {} / 2` is not valid JavaScript: an arrow cannot be the left operand of a division without parentheses around it. What follows a bare arrow's body is a new statement, which may begin with a pattern, so `var q = () => {}` and then a line break and then `/re/.test(s)` emits that literal. Two fixtures pinned the unparseable form and so pinned nothing; both now pin the statement that really follows. `(() => {}) / 2` and `function () {} / 2` divide as they did, and the paren is what makes the first of those an operand.

releases.headline: A virus-scan reply that never says FOUND no longer stalls the scanner
releases.summary: `b.mail.scan`'s ClamAV client read the threat name out of the daemon's reply with a pattern that could be made to take exponential time, and the reply is accepted up to 50 MiB. It reads the name in one pass now. The check that should have caught it read regex literals only and drove them with subjects of one repeated character, so the pattern never reached its costly branch under it. Widening that check is what found this.

items.title: A holder-of-key assertion is readable whatever length the certificate is
items.body:
`b.auth.saml.verifyResponse` refused every holder-of-key confirmation from an identity provider whose certificate encodes to a base64 body whose length is a multiple of 64, answering `auth-saml/hok-bad-cert` on an assertion that is well formed. One certificate in sixteen has such a length, and the length depends only on the certificate, so an affected provider failed every holder-of-key login rather than an occasional one.

The KeyInfo carries the certificate as base64 with whatever whitespace the provider's XML writer used, so the reader strips the whitespace and rewraps the body at 64 columns to hand node a PEM. The rewrap appended a newline to each 64-character group, including the last one when the length divided evenly, and the line before `-----END CERTIFICATE-----` was added on top of it. The blank line that left in the body is what node refused. The groups are joined now, so the body ends where the last group does.

Bearer confirmations were not affected, and neither was the assertion signature check, which reads the provider certificate the operator configured rather than one carried in the assertion. There is nothing to do on upgrade: an assertion that verified before still verifies, and one that was refused for this reason now reaches the possession check it was headed for.

items.title: `b.mail.scan` reads a ClamAV reply in one pass
items.body:
The ClamAV INSTREAM client took the threat name out of `stream: <name> FOUND` with a lazy run between two whitespace quantifiers. A space matches both of them, so on a reply that never says FOUND the engine tries every way of dividing one run of spaces between the two before the match fails. A reply with 2,400 spaces cost 1.8 seconds, and one with 8,192 did not finish within five.

The daemon sends that reply, and it is accepted up to `maxResponseBytes`, which is 50 MiB on the strict profile. So whatever is on the other end of the socket sets the size of that search, whether that is a compromised scanner, something in the path of an unencrypted connection to it, or a reply shaped by the file being scanned.

The reader takes the name in one pass now, and returns the same name the pattern did on every reply shape. Whitespace is the set JavaScript matches rather than the ASCII part of it, so a name wrapped in a non-breaking space is still a name. A name never spans a line, though the spaces around it may, so a label whose spaces cross a line names something on the next one. When a label and the verdict token are separated by nothing but spaces, the name is taken from those spaces, and a threat named `FOUND` is read as the name rather than as the verdict. A reply carrying a clean line and an infected one is read from the infected one, so an infection cannot be downgraded to clean. A check compares the reader against the pattern it replaced across 27,335 reply shapes, which is every sequence of up to seven of the pieces a reply is made of.

There is nothing to do on upgrade. Verdicts, threat names and audit records are unchanged.

items.title: Six credential and command readers no longer slow on a run of spaces
items.body:
The widened check found the same shape in five more places, all reading attacker-supplied text. Three were found first: the `Bearer` credential in `b.middleware.scimServer`, the same credential in `b.middleware.attachUser`, and the arguments of an IMAP `NOTIFY SET` command in `b.mail.server`.

Each spelled the value it wanted as `(.+)` after `\s+`. Both accept a space, so text made of the scheme or command and a long run of spaces can be divided between them at every space, and the engine tries every division before the match fails. Measured on each: about 5ms at 4,096 characters and between 72ms and 78ms at 16,384, which is four times the input for fifteen times the work.

All three now require the value to start at a character that is not a space, which is the only division there is. At 16,384 characters they take under a millisecond. What they read is unchanged for every value that is not made entirely of spaces; one that is reads as absent rather than as a value made of spaces, so `scimServer` answers a header of `Bearer` and nothing but spaces with the same `Missing Bearer token` it gives a header with no credential at all, rather than passing a string of spaces to the token callback.

The `scimServer` header is already refused above 8 KiB before the pattern runs, which bounds what that one could cost. The `attachUser` reader is the one the check cannot see, since its pattern is built from the scheme rather than written out, and it carries a test of its own.

Three more came out of the same check once it could reach a pattern's costly branch: the `FETCH` and `UID` command readers in `b.mail.server`'s IMAP listener, and the reader that takes the options off an IMAP command written with a parenthesised list. Each measured 20ms at 8,192 characters and grew fifteenfold for four times the input, and each is reading a command off the socket before the session is authenticated. They take the same form as the other three now.

There is nothing to do on upgrade.

items.title: `b.mtlsCa.parseGeneration` reads a subject DN in one pass
items.body:
The widened check found a second pattern. `parseGeneration` read the `OU=CAv{N}` generation tag out of a certificate's subject with `(?:^|[\r\n]|(?<!\\)[,+])\s*OU=CAv(\d+)`. A newline is both an RDN separator and whitespace, so on text where separators and spaces run together, every separator is a start position and the `\s*` after it scans the rest of the run before failing: 8,192 characters cost 22ms and 32,768 cost 360ms.

A certificate does not deliver that text today. Node renders a subject as one `type=value` per line and escapes a newline inside a value as `\0A`, so the character after a separator is the next attribute type and the `\s*` matches nothing. The reading no longer rests on that escaping: the DN is split on its separators and each field is read from its own start, once. At 32,768 characters it takes 0.07ms.

What it reports is unchanged, including the two cases the lookbehind was there for: an escaped `\,` or `\+` inside a value does not separate, and a multi-valued RDN joined with `+` does. A check builds a certificate for every subject that up to three of the pieces a DN is made of can produce, 1,884 of them, and requires the reader to answer on each what the pattern answered.

There is nothing to do on upgrade.

items.title: Vendored PKI bundle moves to 0.6.51
items.body:
`lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` carries `@blamejs/pki` 0.6.51, up from the 0.6.30 that shipped in 0.19.2. This is shipped code: `b.mtlsCa` and `b.auth.passkey` run it.

Three of the versions bind an enrollment to the connection it is sent on. 0.6.31 reports the RFC 5929 `tls-unique` value of a TLS 1.2 connection and accepts a request body built from it, per RFC 7030 section 3.5. 0.6.32 lets `simpleenroll` and `simplereenroll` take a CSR builder, so the CSR is signed over the `tls-unique` of the connection that carries it rather than of an earlier one. 0.6.33 adds the RFC 9266 `tls-exporter` binding for TLS 1.3, 32 bytes under the label `EXPORTER-Channel-Binding`; it is withheld below TLS 1.3, where RFC 9266 section 2 also requires the RFC 7627 extended master secret that Node gives no way to confirm.

The rest refuse things they used to accept. 0.6.34 reports an injected transport that does not return a promise as a typed option error naming the option, in every client that takes one. 0.6.35 through 0.6.37 refuse a natively signed C509 certificate that spells an extension, an algorithm or a value in a redundant form instead of the registry entry naming the same thing, so a certificate has one encoding and an issuer signature cannot cover two different C509 byte strings. 0.6.38 lets a trust anchor name the namespace its root is trusted for, and `pki.path.validate` enforces that as the initial name-constraint state. 0.6.39 builds a verdict with its fields rather than writing them on afterward, so a value left on `Object.prototype` cannot answer a question the verification never asked, and a verdict ends the prototype lookup for `then` so an accessor installed there cannot rewrite it between the verification and the caller. 0.6.40 carries that through the rest of the toolkit: the verdicts of `attrcert.verify`, `crl.verify`, `csr.verify`, the two `ct` signature-timestamp verbs, `path.validate` and `webauthn.verify` are each built rather than written onto, and a list a verdict reports is appended to by defining the entry rather than assigning it, so a setter at the appended index cannot take the value. Path validation, CMS verification, timestamp verification, CMP protection verification and Sigstore bundle verification append to their lists the same way. 0.6.41 does the same for the tables the toolkit looks names up in: `pki.C.TIME`, `pki.C.BYTES`, `pki.C.LIMITS`, `pki.C.NAMES` and the name tables under it, `pki.asn1.TAGS` and the ASN.1 builder tables carry no prototype, so a name taken off the wire resolves to an entry the table registered or to nothing. Two verbs could be reached that way, `webauthn.verify` among them. 0.6.42 lets `pki.trust.anchor` carry the namespace a root program trusts a root for as `opts.nameConstraints`, which `pki.path.validate` applies as the initial name-constraint state even where the root certificate itself states no such limit, and refuses a subtree whose base does not match the form its tag names.

The nine after it are additions and one correction. 0.6.43 orders path building through a mesh of cross-certified domains by the two RFC 4158 section 3.5 name heuristics; it is ordering alone, so no candidate is removed and every assembled path still goes through `pki.path.validate`. A bounded search spends its budget on whichever branches the order steers it to, so a build that now reports `path/build-limit` wants a larger `opts.maxCandidatesConsidered`. 0.6.44 reaches a certification authority through a forward proxy that authenticates with RFC 7616 Digest. 0.6.45 validates a path reaching a certificate signed with the RFC 9802 stateful hash-based algorithm, and holds a certificate carrying an HSS, XMSS or XMSS^MT key to that specification's key-usage rule. 0.6.46 checks a Sigstore bundle against the certificate-transparency logs that recorded the signing certificate, for an operator who supplies their keys as `opts.ctLogs`. 0.6.47 lets a CMP enrollment left waiting be picked up by a later process through a resume token. 0.6.48 authenticates a CMC enrollment request with a shared secret instead of a signature. 0.6.49 answers an authority's encrypted challenge for a key that cannot sign for itself, and opens a CMS key-agreement recipient whose encrypted key is not the first one listed. 0.6.50 protects a CMP message with a KEM-based message authentication code. 0.6.51 holds a declared `senderKID` to the key that verified the protection, so a CMP message naming one key and signed under another is refused.

There are no API changes and nothing to do on upgrade. The bundle ships with no dependencies and no install hooks, and its recorded SHA-256 is checked against the file on every build.

items.title: The lexer identifies which text is a pattern
items.body:
The check found patterns by matching slashes across a line. Whether a `/` opens a pattern or divides two numbers or sits inside a string is a lexing question, and answering it with a search over the line got it wrong in both directions: across `lib/`, 4,443 spans that are comment prose, URL paths inside strings and `/* */` openers were measured as patterns, while ten real ones were not found at all. `tok.replace(/~1/g, "/").replace(/~0/g, "~")` is the second kind: the scan takes `/").replace(/` as a span, which carries off the opening slash of the pattern after it.

The embedded WebAuthn attestation roots are where that showed. A base64 line of a certificate contains slashes, and the text between two of them parses as a pattern whose two `+` quantifiers measure superlinear once a probe reaches them, so the check was on course to report a certificate as a slow regular expression.

The framework already contains a lexer, and the comment rule already shares its classifier with the tool that sweeps comments. The linear-time check now uses that lexer, and reads the 893 pattern literals `lib/` actually holds, 597 of them distinct.

A lexer emits a template literal as one token, so a pattern written inside a substitution sits within that token and reaches nothing reading pattern tokens. The code between `${` and its matching brace is read in turn, to any depth, and the offsets are carried through so a report still points at the line the pattern is on. Where a substitution ends is found by lexing it, and by counting its braces when the lexer finds no closing brace at all. Counting skips strings and nothing else, so a brace written in a comment, a pattern or a nested template raises its depth: `${/[{]/.test(s)}` counts two opens and one close and runs to the end of the file, and `${1 /* { */}` walks past the real end and accepts a `}` written in a line comment further down, swallowing every pattern in between. Counting is kept as the second answer because a lexer that reads one token wrongly there finds no closing brace and loses the rest of the file, where a count that is wrong about a quoted brace still stops nearby. Whether a `${` is escaped is decided by whether the run of backslashes before it is odd, since `\\${` opens a substitution while `\${` does not.

Lexer corrections came with it, all of the same shape: a statement may begin with a pattern, and the tokenizer read the slash that starts one as division. That happens after the `)` of a control-flow header, and after `else` and `do`, each of which governs a statement that need not be braced. A `}` that closed an object closed an expression, so the slash after it divides, while one that closed a block ended a statement. The body of a function or class EXPRESSION closes a value the same way, so `var x = function () {} / 2` divides where a declaration's body ends a statement; read as a block, that slash opened a pattern and ran to the opening slash of the next real one. Which one a body is depends on where its keyword stands, so it is settled at the `{` by the same reading, including the cases that look like an expression and are not: a restricted-production keyword with a line terminator after it has already ended its statement, and `export` or `default` introduces a declaration. `async` is a modifier on the keyword rather than a position of its own, so the position is the one before it, and only while nothing separates the two: `var f = async` with the `function` on the next line is an assignment followed by a declaration. What separates them is looked for in the text between the two tokens rather than in the whitespace run before the second, since a comment can carry the line terminator and `async /*` newline `*/ function` is separated by it. The walk back to that keyword skips a bracketed group whole rather than naming the forms one may take, since a superclass is an expression and can be written `extends ns["Base"]`, `extends mixin(Base)`, `extends null` or `extends import("x").constructor`. A superclass may also be a function or class expression of its own, and the keyword after such a body owns THAT body, so the walk steps over it and carries on to the one whose body it is classifying. A word right after `class` or `function` is that thing's NAME whatever word it is spelled like, so `class of {}` and `function* of() {}` are read through, but `extends` is the heritage keyword rather than a name: what follows it is the superclass expression, so a brace directly after it opens an object and `class extends {} {}` has its body in the second pair. The walk is bounded by the token list rather than by a count of its own, which stopped before the keyword of a superclass written as a long member expression. A pattern is a value literal like a number or a string, so one may stand in a superclass too.

A name may begin outside ASCII, and the tokenizer read only ASCII, so it skipped the character and the slash after such a name opened a pattern rather than dividing; it asks what is NOT part of a name now, as the reader beside it does. That question is only as good as what counts as a space, and only the few spaces that are typed most often did: a no-break space, a form feed or a byte-order mark before a pattern statement became the start of a name, and the slash after it divided. Whitespace is the set the language names, which is tab, vertical tab, form feed, the `Zs` category and the byte-order mark, alongside the line terminators. A line continuation inside a string is a backslash and the terminator after it, and `\` followed by CRLF is three characters: advancing two left the newline to end the string, so the real closing quote opened another one and swallowed what came after.

The tables this lexer looks words up in carry no prototype now. `KEYWORDS["constructor"]` found `Object.prototype.constructor`, so every identifier spelled `constructor`, `toString`, `valueOf` or `hasOwnProperty` tokenized as a keyword and the slash after one was read as whatever that keyword implies rather than as the division that follows a name. The tables that compare against 1 were shielded by that comparison rather than by design, which is not a difference worth resting on. which a brace is cannot be read off the brace, so it is decided at the matching `{` by the classifier the comment stripper in the same file already used, two answers to one structural question having drifted apart. What that classifier is told about a preceding colon matters too: a colon separating a property from its value or closing a ternary is followed by a value, while one ending a label or a `case` is followed by a statement, and `label: {}` opens a block. So does a keyword that forbids a line terminator after it once one appears: `yield` on its own line has ended its statement, and the brace below opens a block rather than the object it would otherwise yield. A postfix `++` or `--` ends an expression, so the slash after it divides; reading it as a pattern opener swallowed the rest of the line and took the opening slash of the next real pattern with it. Which form it is depends on whether there was something to operate on, whether a line terminator came between, since one ends the statement and leaves the operator to start the next, and whether the paren before it closed a control-flow header rather than an expression. A prefix one is followed by its operand, which may itself begin with a pattern. A line comment ends at every line terminator and not only at a newline, and the two Unicode ones are whitespace like the rest: a lexer that skips them as unknown leaves no gap between the statements they separate, and one that reads past them swallows the rest of the file as a comment. `debugger` is a whole statement, so a pattern may begin on the line after it; left out of the keyword table it read as an identifier, and an identifier divides, so the pattern following one reached the check as no token at all. Which keywords a pattern may follow is read from one table now, the one the comment stripper beside it already used. The tokenizer carried its own chain of comparisons, and the two had drifted by five words: `debugger`, `extends` and `default` were each found missing separately, and `try` and `finally` were missing too and had not been found at all. `break` and `continue` take a label and nothing else, and nothing divides a label, so a slash after either the keyword or the label it carries opens a pattern; with the semicolon left to insertion, the pattern on the next line is the next statement, and reading that slash as division emitted no pattern token for it at all. The header case is now decided at the matching `(`, which is where the comment stripper beside it already decided the same question. It reads through the transparent word in `for await (`, and a control keyword used as a property name does not open a header, since `obj.if(x) / 2` divides. `of` is read the same way from the other side: it is a keyword only inside a `for (x of y)` header, so anywhere else it is an ordinary name and `var of = 4; of / 2` divides, as does `if (of / 2)`. Which word opened a paren is tracked beside whether one did, so a rule can ask which header it is inside. It has to be the RELATION of such a header rather than anything inside a `for`, since `for (of / 2; false;)` puts it in a traditional header's initializer where it is a name, so the token before it must be the binding target: a name, or the bracket or paren that closes a destructured or parenthesised one. `await` and `yield` are read the same way: an operator inside an async function body and a generator body, and in a script an ordinary name, so `var await = 4; await / 2` and `var yield = 4; yield / 2` divide. Both are asked of the INNERMOST function body, since an ordinary function nested inside an async one resets the grammar; and a method NAMED `async` is not an async method, which is told apart by whether a name or an arrow follows the word. The lexer now also reads the `v` flag, which it stopped before, leaving the flag to be read as a name and the pattern rebuilt without it. That flag enables character classes that nest, which this reader does not parse, so a pattern using it is reported unmeasured with that reason rather than measured under a shape that might not be the one that runs. The framework has no such pattern today.

items.title: A pattern after `await` or `yield` is read in the body it sits in
items.body:
Whether `await` is an operator or a name depends on the function body around it, and the reader found that body only where a brace opened one. A concise arrow body has no brace, so `const f = async x => await /(?:a+)+$/.test(x)` read the `await` as a name, the slash after it as division, and emitted no pattern for the linear-time check to measure. A concise body now runs to the end of its expression: a `;`, a `,` at the arrow's own depth, the colon of a conditional it sits inside, a closer that carries the depth below it, or an inserted semicolon, which a line break makes before a word, a `{`, a `!`, a `~`, a prefix `++` or `--`, a number or a string, and after a postfix `++` or the brace closing an arrow body also before a `(`, a `[` or a template.

The reader also missed function bodies whose header it could not follow back. A member may be named with any reserved word, a string, a number or a computed expression, and the modifier that makes it async or a generator stands before that name: `{ async catch() {} }`, `{ *[Symbol.iterator]() {} }`, `{ async "s"() {} }` and `{ async async() {} }` are all read now. `async` immediately before an arrow is that arrow's parameter rather than a modifier, and the walk stops at the arrow before the one it is reading, so the inner arrow of `async x => y => …` takes no modifier from the outer one. A control header's parens are not a parameter list and neither are a call's, so `if (x) { await … }` and `g()` followed by a bare block are read in the body around them; a member list holds no statements, so the parens of `{ catch() {} }` are a parameter list; and a class body is found through a superclass written as a member expression, including `class C extends ns.default {}`.

A template substitution holds an expression written in the grammar around the template, and it was read on its own: every `await` and `yield` inside one was a name. The body around the template is carried into both the reading of the substitution and the search for where it ends, so `` `${await /}(a+)+$/.test(s)}` `` no longer ends at the brace written inside the pattern, and a substitution that begins with a brace opens an object rather than a block.

A `for` header binds a name however the name is spelled, so `for (let async of xs)` binds `async` and iterates over `xs`; the word before the relation was required to be an ordinary name, which left the binding as the relation and the relation as a name. `let` is a declaration keyword at the head of a `for` header and where a statement begins, and an ordinary name elsewhere, so `y => let` ends an expression.

Which forms hold is checked by crossing them rather than by listing them: the modifiers, names, parameter lists and hosts a function header can be written with; the contexts a concise arrow can stand in, in both directions; the block forms and what can precede them; the substitution forms and the bodies they sit in; and the `for` headers crossed with every reserved word as the binding name. What no parser accepts is skipped, so the crossings need no list of exclusions.

items.title: Reading a run of templates costs the templates, not the file
items.body:
Finding where a substitution ends lexed the whole rest of the source, and every nested template in that remainder lexed its own remainder again. A file of 1,280 one-substitution templates took 11.4 seconds, growing about eightfold for each doubling. The lexer stops at the brace that ends the substitution, and the same file reads in under a second.

Building a subject to drive a pattern runs matches against pieces of that pattern, in the process that reports on it rather than in the child that carries a deadline. Those pieces can backtrack the way the pattern does: thirty optional characters ahead of a required run of them takes every subset, and one such pattern had not returned after 45 seconds. What may run is decided by the paths it can take. A quantifier on a group is refused, and quantified single tokens are refused once the ways they can split the candidate exceed a million. A pattern that cannot be driven is reported unmeasured instead of stopping the run.

items.title: The live-backend gate can reach the backends it names
items.body:
A release runs the live integration tests for the backends whose files it touched, and which files belong to which backend is a table of path prefixes. Fourteen of those prefixes named a path no file has. Eleven were the federation entry, which named `lib/oauth`, `lib/saml`, `lib/openid`, `lib/ciba`, `lib/jar`, `lib/oid4v` and `lib/scim` for modules that sit under `lib/auth/` and `lib/middleware/`, so no OAuth, SAML, OIDC, CIBA or SCIM change has ever selected the Keycloak backend. Three more named modules that are gone.

The check standing behind that table asked whether every integration test file belongs to some entry, which the federation test did: the entry claimed it and could not be reached. A prefix that matches no file under `lib/` is refused now, so an entry that cannot be selected stops the release rather than passing quietly.

The prefixes point at the paths the modules have. `jarm`, `par`, `dcr`, `lib/mail-smtp` and `lib/network-ntp` named no module and were removed.

The squash message a merge writes is derived from the local release notes, while everything gating that merge asks the remote about the pull request. A dirty tree or a stale checkout could therefore put a description on `main` of something other than what was merged, so the merge refuses unless the working tree is clean and the local head is the head that was reviewed, and the merge itself is bound to that head, so a branch that moves between the check and the merge stops it rather than landing under a description of the tree that was checked.

items.title: Composed patterns are measured for linear time
items.body:
The linear-time check extracts regex literals from the source. A pattern built with `new RegExp("...")`, or through a helper that wraps one, is not a literal, so 33 of them went unmeasured. That included every entry in the table `b.guardSql` matches statements against, which is the one place in the framework a regex is pointed at hostile SQL by design.

Both shapes are reconstructed and measured now: a direct `new RegExp` on a string, and a one-argument helper that wraps `new RegExp` with fixed flags. A pattern assembled from a variable or a `join()` cannot be rebuilt without running the file, and is still left to the module's own tests.

All 33 measure linear. Four of them are refused by `b.guardRegex.assertSafe`, which is the framework's own conservative screen; they now carry a measurement rather than an assertion.

items.title: The text a pattern reached by is preserved as written
items.body:
Two ways of reading a pattern lost part of it before it was measured.

A group offering a choice was read by taking one branch. Which branch a pattern can actually take is not always decidable from the text before it: an assertion inside a branch can read what precedes it, what follows it, or the quantified body the reading stops short of, and three ways of deciding it each got a different shape wrong. So the choice is no longer made. Every branch is read, and the probe drives all of them. The branch that reaches the body drives it, and the ones that cannot fail at once.

A pattern given to the constructor as a string is re-spelled as a literal so pattern and flags can be told apart. Every slash in it was escaped, including one the pattern had already escaped. `new RegExp("^(?:\\/|/)+$")` became a pattern matching a backslash and a slash on one side and a slash on the other, so two alternatives that were the same alternative stopped being the same, and a pattern that backtracks exponentially read as fast. A slash the pattern escapes is left as it is, and one inside a character class is left alone too, since a literal does not escape it there.

items.title: A pattern is driven past its opening literal
items.body:
Subjects were built from one character repeated. A pattern that opens with a literal fails at that token on such a subject and never reaches what follows it, so a costly body behind `\bCOPY\b` was never reached and read as fast. The prefix a pattern requires is now read off it verbatim, punctuation included, and seeded into subjects of its own. Where a pattern requires several literals in order, the runs joined in order are seeded too. A subject carrying one of them stops at the next.

The filler is drawn from the pattern itself. `a` and a space do not enter a body that accepts only `x`, and some ambiguity needs a motif rather than a character: `(?:ab|ab)+$` costs on `ab` repeated and returns at once on either letter alone. Each subject is also tried with a trailing character the pattern cannot accept. A pattern only backtracks on its way to failing.

The characters a repetition consumes are chosen before the rest, and a cap no longer costs one of them. The filler list was capped and filled in order, so whatever came first spent it: `^PREFIX(z+)+$` got `a`, a space, and four letters of its prefix and never `z`, and `^(?:a+|b+|c+|d+|e+|f+|g+|h+|(?:z+)+)$` spent it on eight cheap branches before reaching the costly one, so every subject stayed in an alternative that returns at once. A character a repetition consumes is taken whatever precedes it, and so is what a quantified GROUP repeats: six compound motifs in front of the costly branch spent a fixed allowance and left `^(?:(?:a-)+|(?:b-)+|(?:c-)+|(?:d-)+|(?:e-)+|(?:f-)+|(?:z@|z@)+)$` without `z@`. What the pattern names elsewhere is opportunistic and keeps the room it had.

Which character a token accepts is asked of the engine rather than read off the token's own letters. `\d` names a set that the letter `d` is not in, and `\x7a` is the character `z`, so a filler taken from the text enters neither. An escape is read as one token for the same reason: split into `\x`, `7` and `a` it yields two characters the pattern refuses. A negated class is entered by a character it does not list, which is found the same way.

Where a token names a SET, a member of it is chosen rather than the reading stopping there. That is one rule covering what were four separate holes. An escape names a character, so `^\x50REFIX(z+)+$` requires `PREFIX` and not `xREFIX`. A class still requires one character, so `^[A-F]PREFIX(z+)+$` requires `APREFIX` rather than nothing at all. A group that carries no quantifier is required too, so `^(?:A|A)PREFIX(z+)+$` requires `APREFIX` where the reading used to stop at the parenthesis; a lookaround is the exception, since it matches without taking anything, and `^(?!X)...` requires no `X` at all. A backreference names what a capture matched rather than a digit, so `(?:(a-|a-)\1)+$` is driven with `a-a-`; the groups that capture nothing are not counted, or the numbering shifts and the reference names the wrong text. A motif is what a quantified group repeats and need not be a word, so `(?:a-|a-)+$` is driven with `a-`, which it costs on, rather than with either character alone, which it returns at once on. A quantifier inside an alternative does not fix its length, but one instance of the piece it repeats is a length the alternative accepts, so the compound survives rather than being abandoned: `(?:a-b+|a-b+)+$` is driven with `a-b`. A counted range is read the same way, its lower bound standing as the representative, so `(?:a{2,3}b|a{2,3}b)+$` is driven with `aab`. A count of exactly zero is the other direction: the piece is never consumed, so it leaves the motif rather than standing in it, and `(?:a{0}-b|a{0}-b)+$` is driven with `-b` rather than with an `a-b` the alternative refuses. How deeply a motif sits inside ordinary groups no longer decides whether it is read: each nested reading takes a strictly shorter piece of text, so the recursion is bounded by the pattern's own length, and a cutoff at four groups answered `(?:(?:(?:(?:(?:(?:a-|a-))))))+$` with nothing. A group nested inside the alternative offers a choice of its own, and an assertion in a branch can refuse it, so every branch becomes a motif rather than the first that spells something: `(?:(?:(?!a)a|b)-|(?:(?!a)a|b)-)+$` is driven with `b-` as well as `a-`. Where there are several such groups the viable branch is not at the same index in each, so the combinations across them are built rather than one index shared by all: `(?:(?!a)a|b)(?:c|(?!d)d)-` needs `bc-`, which sharing an index reaches by no route. The product of those combinations is exponential in the number of groups and is capped, and it counts up from the first branch of every group, so a cap leaves the last groups on their first branch in everything it builds. The reading with every group on the SAME branch is therefore built whatever the cap: seven copies of `(?:(?!a)a|b)` need `bbbbbbb`, which the product reaches only as its last combination of 128. Sampling reaches no vector that is neither near the start of the product nor all on one branch, so one further reading answers each group on its own, by taking the first branch that accepts what it spells. A branch whose assertion contradicts its own literal, `(?!a)a`, does not. What the groups before it produced is part of that question, since a lookbehind reads it: `(?<!a)c` accepts `c` at the start of a candidate on its own and refuses it after an `a`, so a branch checked in isolation was accepted for a position it cannot occupy. A branch can also be settled by text AFTER its group, which nothing deciding one group at a time can see: in `(?:a(?!-)|b(?=-))-` the `-` that follows decides it. So the finished motif is put to the alternative itself, and where it is refused whole combinations are tried until one is accepted. The combination is the unit because two groups can need to move together, and trying one at a time finds neither. Both readings run a branch or an alternative and never the whole pattern, and only text carrying no quantifier on a group, since those are the shapes this is all here to find. A quantifier on that nested group is read the way one on a single piece is, so `(?:(?:ab){2}c|(?:ab){2}c)+$` is driven with `ababc` rather than dropping the compound. That is what reached the three IMAP readers above. And a class inside a motif is a set too, so `(?:a\d|a\d)+$` is driven with `a0`. In each case the old reading stopped at the token, no subject satisfied the anchor, and the body behind it was entered by nothing.

A seed comes from what a pattern MATCHES rather than from how it is spelled: backslashes used to be stripped, which made `u03A9` a word of `[Ω]` and `bCOPY` one of `\bCOPY`, and a subject starting with either fails the anchor. The empty string is always among the seeds, tried after the specific ones. It is the whole subject for a pattern with no literal in it, and it is the only subject that reaches a body behind an alternative the prefix did not take, as in `^(?:X|(?:,-|,-)+)$`. A class is answered by a member of itself, read off the class, so `(?:[q]|[q])+$` is driven with `q` and `(?:[Ω]|[Ω])+$` with the character it names, whatever its codepoint; a motif is bounded by what a subject can carry rather than by a short fixed length, so `(?:abcdefg|abcdefg)+$` is driven with the seven characters it costs on; `\cA` is control-A rather than the letter `c`; a pattern with no literal in it at all, like `^(?:,-|,-)+$`, is driven with its motif alone, where before the motif was derived and then never used; and a group nested inside an alternative contributes the string it matches, so `(?:a(?:b|b)|a(?:b|b))+$` is driven with `ab`, its alternation divided at the group's own bar rather than at every bar in it; a fixed quantifier keeps an alternative fixed-length, so `(?:ab{2}|ab{2})+$` is driven with `abb`; and a fixed quantifier in a required prefix repeats what it follows, so `^A{2}PREFIX(z+)+$` requires `AAPREFIX`; and a Unicode property escape is one token naming a set, read under the flag that makes it one, so `(?:\p{Letter}0|\p{Letter}0)+$` is driven with a letter and a zero rather than with the letters of the word `Letter`. A set whose members lie outside any range worth walking is searched for rather than looked up in a list of scripts someone thought to write down, so `\p{Script=Adlam}` is answered too.

The pieces a subject is built from are assembled by one function now. Fifty-eight patterns of these shapes are driven through it and each is asserted to be given a character its body repeats, forty-four pin the prefix a pattern requires, four pin that no seed is built from a pattern's spelling, and the claim underneath them is checked over 312 generated shapes: the prefix a pattern requires is a string that pattern accepts, and one that does not already match it.

Where a group offers a choice, every branch of it is read rather than the first one that spells a literal, and every such group is read rather than only the first. Which branch a pattern can take is not always decidable from the text before it, since an assertion inside one can read what precedes it, what follows it, or the quantified body the reading stops short of. So the choice is not made: each branch becomes a subject of its own, the one that reaches the body drives it, and the ones that cannot fail at once. Reading only the first group's first four branches left two families measured by nothing, each found by moving the branch that reaches the body through every position: a fifth branch was never built, and a group after the first was never varied, which left `^A(?:x|x)L(?:P(?!z)|Q(?=z))(z+)+$` reading as fast although it takes 892ms on `AxLQ`. One group varies per reading, since enumerating combinations across groups is exponential, but every group is varied and every branch of it: that is one walk per group per branch, which is linear in the pattern. Stopping at four groups left the fifth of `^(?:A|A)(?:A|A)(?:A|A)(?:A|A)(?:B(?!X)|C(?=X))X(z+)+$` never varied, so the only prefix that reaches its body was built by nothing, and a bound of twelve branches never built branches twelve through nineteen of the two widest alternations in `lib/`. For scale, of the 597 patterns `lib/` holds, 517 offer no choice at all, the most any offers is three groups, and the widest offers twenty branches. One further reading takes, in every group, the first branch the pattern still accepts. It reaches a prefix that needs a later branch in several groups at once, which varying one group at a time cannot: `^(?:(?!A)A|B)(?:(?!C)C|D)(z+)+$` requires `BD`, and one-at-a-time offers `BC` and `AD`, each refused by its own lookahead. It is one more reading rather than a replacement, because choosing per group is wrong wherever an assertion reads forward past the prefix: `^(?:A(?=X)|B(?!X))X` refuses `A` on the prefix alone and takes `B`, which the literal after the group then contradicts. Both readings are kept and both are driven.

A pattern offers a choice at its own top level too, and the costly branch is not always the first. `^SAFE$|^AB-CD(z+)+$` was read up to the bar and required `SAFE`, so nothing built `AB-CD`. Each top-level alternative is a pattern in its own right and each is walked as one, the prefixes pooled. Every one of them is walked rather than the first few: these are the pattern's own branches rather than a search space, so the cost is linear in the size of the pattern, and a cap dropped the costly branch of a pattern carrying two dozen cheap ones in front of it.

A count is read for what it requires, and the prefix carries that. The lower bound is that number, so `^A{17}PREFIX(z+)+$` requires seventeen of them where a cutoff at sixteen stopped before the prefix, and `^A{1,3}X(z+)+$` requires one where a range used to end the prefix at the brace. Zero requires nothing and the walk carries on past it, so `^A{0}-P(z+)+$` requires `-P` rather than nothing at all. A count on a GROUP is read the same way, so `^(?:AB){2}PREFIX(z+)+$` requires `ABABPREFIX` and `^(?:AB){0}-P(z+)+$` requires `-P`. A count with the upper bound left open, `{n,}`, is a count like any other and was read as a literal brace, so `^A{2,}X(z+)+$` requires `AAX`. How much text a prefix or a motif may carry is the size of the subjects the probe builds, 8,192 characters, rather than a number a real pattern reaches: at forty a prefix written out as forty-one characters was cut short, and a cut-short prefix is worse than none, since every subject built from it fails the anchor and the body behind it is driven by nothing while the check reports fast. A motif is bounded the same way, so the sixty-five character unit `(?:ba{64}|ba{64})+$` repeats is kept.

Past that size the probe cannot drive the pattern at all, and it says so. A required prefix longer than a subject reports the pattern as one the check could not measure, which is reported rather than passed, on the same footing as a probe that ran out of time. The same holds for the other thing it can fail to build: where an alternative offers choices and no reading produced a unit the pattern accepts, nothing built repeats what it repeats, and the enumeration is exponential in the number of groups so a budget is always reachable. Refusing to look is kept apart from a refusal: the check declines to run text carrying a quantifier on a group, and declining is not a verdict. That is the difference the sequence of caps kept getting wrong: declining to answer is a result, and answering with a prefix known to be short is not. One reader answers what a `{...}` spells now, rather than four that had to agree. Each expansion is measured before it is built, so a count in the millions costs nothing to refuse.

And the whole of it is checked end to end. Fifty-six patterns that are catastrophic are each driven with the subjects their own pieces build, and each has to measure as costly. Every gap listed above was invisible to a check on the pieces and visible to that one.

That is what found the ClamAV defect above. Reading the prefix as words joined by spaces was not enough on its own: `stream:` keeps its colon only when the prefix is taken verbatim.

items.title: An exemption marker is checked wherever it is written
items.body:
A marker that exempts a line from a rule was validated in `lib/` and `test/` only. Everywhere else the name went unchecked. Five markers had been sitting outside that scope, all naming a class that was renamed so that every use would be re-examined; the rename reached the markers the check could see and left these. None of them exempted anything: the rule they named reads the framework's own source, not those files. They are removed.

The check now reads scripts and the example apps too, skipping installed dependencies and build output. The example app runs a gate of its own with its own classes, so a marker under `examples/` is answered against that registry rather than the framework's; a name in neither is still reported.

items.title: A rule's advertised exemption is the one it honors
items.body:
Each rule carries a header naming the marker that exempts a site. That header is what a reader follows when the build stops on the rule. Ten named a class that had been renamed, so following one produced a marker the repository does not accept. Two more named a class that is registered while the rule never consults it, so the marker was accepted and had no effect, and the build failed again with the message the contributor had just tried to answer.

The ten now name the class they filter on. The two rules take no marker at all, and their headers now state that; their classes are retired, so writing one fails the build rather than being ignored. Eight more rules that never took a marker now state that on the line, which keeps their name and keeps the claim checkable.

A new check holds all of it, and asks the question per rule rather than across the file: a rule may not advertise a retired class, nor a registered class it does not consult, nor a class that is neither registered nor consulted anywhere. The last of these names an exemption no contributor can use.

releases.headline: A documented `schemeAllowlist` that no code read is gone, and two checks hold the reference pages to what the code does
releases.summary: `b.guardMarkdown.validate` documented an option that existed only on its documentation line. Setting it did nothing, and the default it quoted described a constant on a different code path. The line is removed, and a check now compares every documented option against the code that would read it. A second check holds the reference pages to American English.

items.title: `b.guardMarkdown.validate` no longer documents an option nothing reads
items.body:
The option block for `b.guardMarkdown.validate` listed `schemeAllowlist: string[]` with a default of `["http","https","mailto"]`. That name appeared once in the whole framework, on that line. No code read it, so an operator passing `{ schemeAllowlist: ["https"] }` to stop `http:` link targets changed nothing and got no error, and the quoted default described a constant used by `b.guardMarkdown.render` rather than by `validate`.

The line is removed. `validate` has no scheme allowlist. What it has is a fixed dangerous-scheme list, and `dangerousSchemePolicy`, `imageSchemePolicy`, `autolinkSchemePolicy` and `referenceLinkPolicy` decide what happens to a link that carries one of those schemes: `javascript:`, `vbscript:`, `data:`, `blob:`, `jar:`, `tel:` and their neighbors, plus `file:` under `filePolicy`. A scheme outside that list, `http:` included, produces no finding under any of them, so none of them can narrow the set of schemes a document may use.

Nothing to change on upgrade, because the option never had an effect. An operator who set it to keep `http:` links out of a document was not getting that, and validation still does not offer it. The one place the framework holds link targets to a scheme set is `b.guardMarkdown.render`, which emits only `http`, `https`, `mailto` and relative references.

items.title: `b.auth.oauth.parseJarmResponse` documents the options it accepts
items.body:
The page listed `acceptedAlgs` and `maxClockSkewMs`. Neither reaches the JWT verification: the JARM response's signature is checked with a fixed set of options, and neither name appears anywhere in the framework's code. An operator narrowing the algorithms a JARM response may be signed with, or tightening the clock skew, changed nothing about how the response was verified and got no error saying so.

Both are removed. The page now lists `requireIssParam`, which the function does accept and forward, and which it had not documented.

If you were passing either removed option, verification was already running with the framework's own algorithm set and skew; nothing about how a response is verified changes here, only what the page claims.

items.title: Two pages no longer document a positional argument as an option
items.body:
`b.mail.bimi.validateTinyPsSvg` carried an option block listing `svgBytes: Buffer | string`, and `b.consent.recognizedPurpose` one listing `name: string`. Both take that value as their first positional argument, which their signature lines already show, and `recognizedPurpose`'s own example calls it as `b.consent.recognizedPurpose("educational-only")`. Following the option block instead gave `validateTinyPsSvg({ svgBytes: buf })`, an object that is neither a Buffer nor a string.

Both option blocks are removed. Pass the value directly.

items.title: A documented option must appear in the code
items.body:
Every option named in a reference page's option block is now compared against the framework's own source, and a name that appears nowhere in the code fails the build. An option is often handed to a helper in another file, so the check reads the whole tree rather than the declaring file.

The check asks whether the name occurs in the code, not whether the code honors the option. Options here are consumed through profile, mapping and rule tables as often as through a direct property read, and those are indistinguishable from a text search.

Option blocks are written five ways across the framework: a typed line each, an inline object, a brace-wrapped object, a comma-separated list glossed in prose, and keys qualified by the parameter that carries them. The reader handles all five. A block it takes no options from fails the build too, so a block written a sixth way is reported as unchecked instead of passing. A block that declares no options is left alone.

The existing sibling check reads the option allowlist the code states. This one reads the option block the documentation states. An option can be documented without appearing in an allowlist, so the two cover different surface.

items.title: An option block belongs to a primitive that takes an options object
items.body: A block whose single documented key is also the primitive's single parameter now fails the build. Documenting the fields of an object argument stays correct however that argument is named, so a page listing what an audit event carries is unaffected. What fails is a page that presents the argument itself as a field of an options object.

items.title: Reference-page prose is American English
items.body:
Every documentation block in the framework's source becomes a reference page. Pages reading `behaviour`, `honours`, `recognise`, `normalises`, `defence`, `catalogue`, `analogue`, `ageing`, `canonicalised`, `tunnelling` and their relatives are corrected, across 42 files. A check holds the rest.

The `-ise` family is checked as an exclusion: a word of that shape fails unless it is named as an American one. So `organiser` and `hypothesise` fail without appearing on any list, while `advertise`, `improvisation`, `advisable`, `sunrise` and the `-wise` family pass. A shouted `NORMALISE` is read as prose; a mixed-case `keyCompromise` is read as the identifier it is.

Two kinds of text keep their source spelling and are listed in the check with the reason. An identifier or API value keeps it, because `dual.grant.cancelled` is an emitted event name and the `cancelled` data-subject-request status is part of a documented union. A standard's own wording keeps it, because ISO 18013-5 names the credential a mobile driving licence, and the EU AI Act Art. 50(3) notice text is quoted verbatim beside the `biometric-categorisation` value it pairs with.

items.title: Vendored PKI bundle moves to 0.6.30
items.body:
`lib/vendor/blamejs-pki.cjs` carries `@blamejs/pki` 0.6.30, up from the 0.6.28 that shipped in 0.19.1. This is shipped code: `b.mtlsCa` and `b.auth.passkey` run it.

Two upstream versions land together. 0.6.29 adds a forward HTTP proxy for the EST, ACME and CMP clients, reached through the same `proxy` option the SCEP client already took. 0.6.30 corrects that toolkit's own reference documentation: a mistyped signed-attribute field name, and options and return fields the code accepts or returns that the reference had omitted.

No API changes and nothing to do on upgrade. The bundle ships with no dependencies and no install hooks, and its recorded SHA-256 is checked against the file on every build.

items.title: An audit-guard check deletes a row that exists
items.body:
The Postgres check that a session cannot switch off the append-only guard by setting `blamejs.audit_purge` aimed its DELETE at a counter 50 above the purge boundary. Nothing has to occupy that counter, so on a table whose rows do not reach it the statement matched no row, fired no per-row trigger, and raised nothing. The check reads a raised error as the guard holding, so it failed against a database where the guard was working correctly.

Both the Postgres and MySQL checks now read the highest counter above the boundary and delete from there, so the statement always matches a row and the trigger always runs. This is repository tooling; the guard is unchanged.

items.title: A live rate-limit check stops racing a window boundary
items.body:
The cluster rate-limiter's window is aligned to the epoch, so a one-minute window puts a boundary on every wall-clock minute. The MySQL and Postgres checks took four counted requests in sequence against a real database and asserted the fourth was refused; a sequence that straddled a boundary saw the counter reset and the fourth allowed, failing a check whose subject was the SQL upsert rather than wall-clock timing.

Each sequence now reads the window on both sides of itself and runs again on a fresh key when it turned over, so a sequence that spans a boundary repeats instead of failing. Both still exercise the window-rollover branch by advancing the stored window directly. This is repository tooling; the limiter is unchanged.

items.title: A growth measurement holds up on a loaded machine
items.body: The check that the growth helper separates a linear curve from a quadratic one measured its baseline at 25ms. Scheduler delay adds a fixed amount to both readings, and against a 25ms denominator that was enough to pull a true ratio of 16 below the threshold, so the check failed on a busy machine while nothing it tests was wrong. The baseline is 50ms now, which takes the tolerated delay from about 22ms to about 44ms. This is repository tooling.

items.title: Reference-page wording
items.body: Numeric ranges in the CBOR, PIPL and redirect pages read `28 to 30` rather than using a dash. Sentences in `b.money`, `b.apiKey`, `b.audit`, `b.codepointClass`, `b.logStream`, `b.queue` and `b.auditSign` that carried an aside on a dash, or stated a result as what it costs or buys, now name what happens and to what. None of these change documented behavior.

releases.headline: A JSON Schema `pattern` that is not a regular expression is refused instead of ignored
releases.summary: A `pattern` keyword that failed to compile was skipped, so a typo in a schema silently removed the constraint and every string validated. It is refused at compile time now, the way a pattern with a ReDoS shape already was. Separately, each fuzz harness loads the primitive it fuzzes rather than the whole framework, which is repository tooling and not part of the published package.

items.title: An invalid `pattern` no longer drops the constraint
items.body:
`b.jsonSchema` compiled a `pattern` under the `u` flag, retried without it, and on a string that is not a regular expression under either left the keyword unapplied. `{ pattern: "[" }` therefore accepted every string and reported the instance valid — a schema author's typo removed the one keyword standing between an instance and acceptance, and nothing said so.

The same function already refused a pattern whose SHAPE is a denial-of-service risk, throwing `json-schema/unsafe-pattern` when the schema is compiled. A string that is not a regular expression at all is now refused there too, as `json-schema/invalid-pattern`, and the message quotes the offending pattern so it can be found in a large schema. Patterns are screened across the whole schema when it is compiled, including inside subschemas and `patternProperties` keys, so the error arrives once at compile rather than per instance.

Upgrade note: a schema carrying an uncompilable pattern used to compile and validate; it now throws. A schema whose patterns are valid is unaffected, and the retry without the `u` flag is unchanged — a pattern valid only without it still compiles and still constrains.

The screen follows `$ref` and `$dynamicRef` as it walks, resolving each one through the same registry the validator resolves through. A reference names a location rather than a keyword, and the location can be one the walk does not reach on its own: `contentSchema`, a vendor extension with no keyword at all, a resource named by its URI instead of by a bare fragment, or a document supplied through the `schemas` option. Patterns at those locations reached compile unscreened, so the refusal arrived on the first instance that touched one rather than on the schema, which made it depend on which request came in.

Resolution is scoped the way the specification scopes it. A `$id` starts a new resource, so a fragment inside one names a location in that resource and not the same-named location in the document around it, and a subschema reused under two resources is screened under each. `const` and `enum` hold instance data, so an object sitting in one may carry a `pattern` property that is an ordinary string and is left alone.

The other places the framework compiles a caller-supplied pattern were checked against the same question and were already refusing or failing closed: `b.jsonPath`'s `match()` and `search()` evaluate to false for a pattern they cannot build, `b.flagTargeting` throws on an invalid targeting regex, and the MCP tool-input validator returns a rejection.

items.title: Each fuzz harness loads the primitive it fuzzes
items.body:
Every harness under `fuzz/` opened the package root to reach one guard. The fuzzer instruments each module it loads, so fuzzing one primitive instrumented all 565 — measured, a process starting at between 1487 MB and 1911 MB against its 2048 MB ceiling, which left one target crossing it and reporting an out-of-memory on a 112-byte input its guard refuses in under a millisecond.

The harnesses require their target directly, which is what they exercise. The same target now starts at 256 MB and runs at 337 MB. A check refuses a harness that reaches for the package root again.

Repository tooling only: `fuzz/` is not part of the published package and no runtime behavior changes.

releases.headline: The framework's source carries the comments a reader can check against the code, and nothing else
releases.summary: 60,297 comments come out of `lib/`, about 19% of its lines. What went is narrative: notes about how a decision was reached, what an earlier version did, which review round changed something. A reader opening the file has no way to verify any of it, and none of it describes what the code in front of them does. What stays is what something reads — the licence header, a documentation block carrying a tag, a suppression marker a gate consumes, the note explaining why a block is deliberately empty or why a require is deferred. A new gate refuses the rest, and `b.safeBuffer.hasCrlfOrNul` replaces two hand-rolled header checks the sweep uncovered.

items.title: Narrative comments are removed from the shipped source
items.body:
`lib/` loses 60,297 comments and around 65,800 lines. No behavior changes: every one of them was a comment.

What is kept is what something reads. The licence header. A `/** */` block carrying a tag — the documentation site's page for a primitive IS that block, so those are content. A suppression marker a gate consumes (`allow:`, `eslint-disable`, `c8 ignore`). The comment that is the whole body of a block, because without it `catch (e) { }` is an unexplained swallow. The note recording why a `require` is deferred, which is what the framework's own convention asks for at such a site.

What went was the rest: how a decision was arrived at, what an earlier version did instead, which round of review changed something. A reader has no way to check any of that against the file in front of them, and it doubles the length of what they are reading to get work done.

`node scripts/strip-lib-comments.js --dry-run` reports what would go; `--apply` removes it. A new check refuses a narrative comment reaching `lib/` again, and it shares its classifier with that script rather than restating it, so the sweep and the check cannot disagree about what a comment is.

items.title: `b.safeBuffer.hasCrlfOrNul`
items.body:
Detect CR, LF or NUL in a string. A header field carries all three as one class of problem: CR and LF end the field, and NUL truncates it wherever the value reaches C. Non-string input returns `false`, so the predicate chains without a pre-typecheck, exactly as `b.safeBuffer.hasCrlf` does.

It replaces the same character loop written out twice — once where a multipart part header is parsed out of a body, once where one is serialized into a body. Both refused CR, LF and NUL already; they now ask one primitive.

items.title: Five raw time literals a blind check had been passing over
items.body:
The check that requires a duration to go through `b.constants.TIME` removed a trailing comment from each line only after it had tried to remove regex literals. On a line like `exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 300,` followed by a comment, the slash of the division and the slash opening the comment read as a pattern, so everything between them was discarded and the literal the check exists to find was never examined.

It takes comments off through the lexer now, which is what decides a regex from a division. Five durations were behind that — two in CIBA client assertions, one in the SD-JWT-VC default credential lifetime, two in the SRS day-rotation window — and each is expressed through `b.constants.TIME`. No lifetime changes value.

items.title: A narrative comment in `lib/` is refused
items.body:
`testLibCarriesNoNarrativeComments` walks every file and reports any comment outside the kept classes, naming the file, the line, and the command that removes it.

Finding a comment at all is a lexing question rather than a pattern-matching one — `//` appears inside string literals, regex literals and template interpolations throughout a real codebase, and a regular expression cannot tell those apart from a comment. The check therefore cannot be an entry in the framework's regex-driven pattern catalog, and it reads comment boundaries from the same lexer the sweep uses so the two cannot disagree about what a comment is. Both are repository tooling; neither is part of the published package.
